text: Suppose a company has plants on both sides of the state line. Which workers would {bill} reach?
author: Codex writer B

text: The crew on this side of the line, {presiding}. Our vote can't change the law where the other plant sits.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask the company to start with its addresses. {bill} sets a rule for our state, even if one contract covers several plants.
author: Codex writer B

text: Only our plants, {presiding}. That's part of my objection. The same bargaining team would have to explain different terms to crews doing the same job.
author: Codex writer B

text: Look at the state where each plant operates. I'd vote against {bill} and leave our crews room to bargain over the fee.
author: Codex writer B

text: A worker pays the local but can't vote on the contract. What does {bill} change for that person?
author: Codex writer B

text: The fee could no longer be required to keep the job. {bill} leaves the union's voting rules alone.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd support {bill} for that worker. They could choose whether to pay, and joining the local would still be a separate decision.
author: Codex writer B

text: The worker would keep the option to stay outside the union. My objection to {bill} is what happens to the cost of representing them.
author: Codex writer B

text: It concerns the payment, {presiding}. Whether a nonmember gets a ratification ballot is up to the union's rules.
author: Codex writer B

text: A new grocery clerk sees a notice about monthly union fees. What should the store check if {bill} passes?
author: Codex writer B

text: Check when the new rule covers that agreement. Once it does, {presiding}, the notice can't tell the clerk that paying is a condition of keeping the job.
author: Codex writer B

text: Read the effective date against the agreement, then tell the clerk what payment is voluntary. That's the distinction I'd want {bill} to make clear.
author: Codex writer B

text: Start with the date on the agreement, {presiding}. I oppose the change, but the clerk still deserves a notice they can rely on.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want the store and the steward to read {bill} together before either tells a new hire what they owe.
author: Codex writer B

text: When the plant agreement comes up again, could the union still ask management for a required fee under {bill}?
author: Codex writer B

text: Once {bill} applies to that agreement, they couldn't make paying that fee a condition of employment. They could still ask workers to contribute.
author: Codex writer B

text: The local could ask for voluntary support, {presiding}. A worker who declined it could keep the job. That's what I'm voting for.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's the term {bill} would take off the table. I'd let the people negotiating the contract decide whether to include it.
author: Codex writer B

text: They could ask the membership for money, {presiding}. They'd lose the chance to bargain for a contribution from everyone they represent.
author: Codex writer B

text: If we pass {bill}, does the store start collecting a fee from a new clerk the next morning?
author: Codex writer B

text: No, {presiding}. Lifting the state ban doesn't put a fee in the clerk's agreement. The parties would have to bargain for one.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd tell the clerk to ask for the contract. A vote for {bill} opens a subject for bargaining. It doesn't authorize a deduction from anybody's next check.
author: Codex writer B

text: There'd still have to be an applicable agreement, {presiding}. My vote to keep the ban is about what a future agreement could require.
author: Codex writer B

text: The repeal alone wouldn't collect anything. I oppose {bill} because a required fee could come up the next time that store negotiates.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a fee negotiated after {bill} passes give a nonmember a say in the union's ratification vote?
author: Codex writer B

text: Paying and joining are different decisions, {presiding}. You'd need the local's voting rules to answer for that worker.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd vote for {bill} to let people bargain over representation costs. The local would still decide who gets a ballot under its rules.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's my concern, {presiding}. A worker could help pay for bargaining under an agreement and still be outside the room when the members vote.
author: Codex writer B

text: I wouldn't promise the worker a ballot. {bill} deals with what payment can be required. It gives them no new vote in the local.
author: Codex writer B

text: What would {bill} do to the exception for our plants in a company's national agreement?
author: Codex writer B

text: Read the exception first, {presiding}. If it turns on what state law allows, both sides need to see how that language works after repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want the actual clause in front of me. {bill} changes state law. The words the parties put in their agreement matter too.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the ban, {presiding}. Hand me that contract and I'll show you the words I'd want the workers to ask about.
author: Codex writer B

text: Before voting for {bill}, I'd ask the company and the local to explain the exception to the people working under it. I'm for keeping the ban.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the local asks for a meeting after {bill} passes, does management have to agree to the fee?
author: Codex writer B

text: It has to hear a lawful bargaining proposal where the duty to bargain applies, {presiding}. The two sides can walk out with different positions.
author: Codex writer B

text: No. I support {bill} because it lets them negotiate that term. Management can hear the proposal and make a counteroffer.
author: Codex writer B

text: They wouldn't have to accept it, {presiding}. I'm voting to keep the ban because I don't want continued employment to depend on what they eventually agree.
author: Codex writer B

text: An invitation to bargain isn't a signed contract. My objection to {bill} is that a required payment could end up in that contract later.
author: Codex writer B

text: A company may use one contract from coast to coast. I want somebody taking a job here to know our rule before they sign anything. That's my reason for backing {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Think of the person transferring in from another plant, {presiding}. They shouldn't have to pay a union fee to keep working here just because the company bargains for both plants together.
author: Codex writer B

text: There are people on the payroll who never joined the local. I'd pass {bill} so they can keep working without paying it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Before you tell somebody the fee is worth their money, {presiding}, let them decide. A person can value the contract and still want a choice about paying the local.
author: Codex writer B

text: Picture the grocery clerk reading the notice in the break room on the first day. I'd back {bill} so that clerk can turn down a fee without risking the job.
author: Codex writer B

text: I want a new hire to be able to ask what the local does and then make up their mind about paying. Under {bill} they could say no and finish the shift.
author: Codex writer B

text: Leave pay and hours on the bargaining table, {presiding}. I draw the line at an agreement that makes somebody pay the union to stay employed.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose management and the union both like a fee. Where does that leave the person who just wants to work there? I'd give that person a choice by passing {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: One employer can bargain for several plants at once. Before we pass {bill}, I'd like us to think about the crew that has to explain a state exception to the rest of the local.
author: Codex writer B

text: Stand on either side of a plant gate and you'll hear people talk about what they got in the last contract. I'd vote against {bill} and let those workers negotiate the next one.
author: Codex writer B

text: A nonmember can still need help getting the contract honored. Who pays for that work, {presiding}? I'd leave room for the two sides to settle it.
author: Codex writer B

text: The steward has work to do even for people who didn't join. That's why I can't support {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like the clerk on the late shift to get the same explanation of the deal as the clerk who went to the meeting. We can ask for a plain notice without passing {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: There's a fair question about what the store tells a new employee, {presiding}. My answer would be to show them the agreement and explain the fee. I'd vote against a ban.
author: Codex writer B

text: What could the local bring to the next meeting? With {bill}, we'd be telling both sides to leave one proposal at home. I'd hear it out.
author: Codex writer B

text: Management can already tell the union it doesn't want that term, {presiding}. I see no reason for us to cut off the discussion before they meet.
author: Codex writer B

text: When a company negotiates for plants in several states, somebody has to go through the contract and mark which terms apply here. I'd let the parties reopen that conversation under {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Different plants can have different terms, {presiding}. I'd repeal the ban so the crews here can bargain over their own.
author: Codex writer B

text: A worker can want help enforcing a contract without wanting to join the union. I'd support {bill} so the parties can talk about paying for that help.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who picks up the cost when a nonmember needs representation? Let the local and the employer sit down with that question, {presiding}. That's a reason to repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: Think about who has to explain a new agreement to the night shift. I favor {bill}, and I'd expect a store and its local to spell out any fee they negotiate.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd let the two sides negotiate, {presiding}. Then a clerk who sees a notice about fees could ask both sides to show where the agreement says it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like a union to be able to send the plant manager a proposal and get a meeting about it. That's the change I want from {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the employer bring a counteroffer, {presiding}. As long as the state bars the fee, neither side has a reason to work out terms for one.
author: Codex writer B

text: A national contract can run for years. Before we change the ground under the people working here, I'd ask what the existing exception for their plant says. I'm against {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I don't want a transfer to another plant in this state to start a hunt through the union contract for a fee, {presiding}. I'd keep the ban.
author: Codex writer B

text: If you stay outside the local, you may have no say in its internal decisions. I wouldn't make room for a contract that could still require you to pay it. I'm against {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd protect the person who doesn't join, {presiding}. Access to the contract matters to that worker, and so does being able to decline the fee.
author: Codex writer B

text: A notice goes up and the clerk has to figure out whether the next paycheck will cover the groceries. I'd keep the state ban, {presiding}, so that worker has a choice about paying.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like someone taking their first job to know they can say no to a union payment and keep the job. I wouldn't repeal that protection with {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: People keep saying a fee would have to be negotiated. That's true, {presiding}. It doesn't reassure me about the worker who objects after both sides sign.
author: Codex writer B

text: The employer may well turn down the local's first offer. I'd keep the existing law because what worries me is the fee they might finally agree on after {bill} passes.
author: Codex writer B

text: The same company runs both mills. After {bill} passes, does a crew across the border get the same fee rule as the crew here?
author: Codex writer B

text: Put the national agreement on the desk, {presiding}. How would the payroll office know which plants our vote covers?
author: Codex writer B

text: A worker transfers here without changing employers. Whose law governs the fee at the new plant under {bill}?
author: Codex writer B

text: There's a fee on the pay stub and no ballot in the worker's hand. Which of those things can {bill} change?
author: Codex writer B

text: Help me explain this to the nonmember, {presiding}. What happens to the payment and the vote on the contract?
author: Codex writer B

text: The local has finished counting the ratification votes. For somebody who paid but couldn't vote, what difference would {bill} make?
author: Codex writer B

text: That notice is still hanging beside the store schedule. Before the manager tells a clerk the fee is due, what needs checking under {bill}?
author: Codex writer B

text: Before the grocery puts up its next fee notice, {presiding}, what should the manager and the steward look at together?
author: Codex writer B

text: Say the clerk starts during the old agreement and stays into the new one. How should the store explain the fee when {bill} takes effect?
author: Codex writer B

text: The negotiators have reached the union's proposal on fees. What part could still go into the contract if we adopt {bill}?
author: Codex writer B

text: Where would {bill} leave the bargaining team that wants every worker it represents to help pay?
author: Codex writer B

text: The plant manager asks if keeping the job can still depend on paying the fee. How would you answer under {bill}?
author: Codex writer B

text: The grocery runs payroll on Friday. Would passing {bill} today give the store authority to take a fee out of that check?
author: Codex writer B

text: A clerk comes off the late shift wondering whether the repeal itself starts a payment. Is the vote on {bill} enough?
author: Codex writer B

text: Does this chamber put a fee on anybody's pay stub by lifting the ban, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: A worker helps pay for negotiations, then the local hands out ratification ballots. Would {bill} put one in that worker's hands?
author: Codex writer B

text: Whose rules decide whether a nonmember who pays a fee gets to vote on the deal after {bill}?
author: Codex writer B

text: At the union hall, a nonmember asks whether paying under the new contract gets them a ballot. What can we promise under {bill}?
author: Codex writer B

text: There's a state exception tucked into the national contract. Before we tell the crew what repeal means, what would you want to see, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: The company signed one agreement for plants around the country. How would you settle what its exception means for workers here after {bill}?
author: Codex writer B

text: A steward has the national agreement open to the paragraph about our state. Where should the steward start if we pass {bill}?
author: Codex writer B

text: Management gets a letter asking to bargain over a fee. Does {bill} require the company to sign what the local sends?
author: Codex writer B

text: Once the manager has heard the local out, does {bill} give the union a right to the fee it proposed?
author: Codex writer B

text: Does a place on the bargaining agenda guarantee the local a fee after repeal, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: Before I tell the other crew they're covered, where does {bill} stop?
author: Codex writer B

text: Think of the worker waiting outside while the local counts ballots. What could I tell them {bill} would change?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd hold off on posting that fee notice, {presiding}. What do we need to check first?
author: Codex writer B

text: Could a manager still tell a worker to pay up or lose the job once {bill} covers that contract?
author: Codex writer B

text: Before somebody docks that clerk's pay, show me where {bill} authorizes the deduction. Does it?
author: Codex writer B

text: Say the worker who paid for the bargaining comes to the hall on voting night. Does {bill} get them a ballot?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd hate to give the crew the wrong answer, {presiding}. What does repeal mean for the exception in their national contract?
author: Codex writer B

text: The local wants the fee. The company won't sign. Does {bill} let the local insist on getting its way?
author: Codex writer B
